what_its_for: Bezlotoxumab is a medicine given to help prevent Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) infection from coming back. C. diff is a type of bacterial infection that causes severe diarrhea and stomach problems. This medicine works by blocking a toxin (poison) made by the C. diff bacteria that damages your gut. It is used in adults who are already being treated for C. diff with antibiotics and who are at high risk of getting the infection again.
how_to_take: Bezlotoxumab is NOT a pill or liquid you take by mouth at home. It is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly injected into your vein through an IV line. A healthcare provider will give you this medicine at a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. The infusion takes about 60 minutes. You will only receive ONE single dose of this medicine during your C. diff treatment. You do not take it daily — it is a one-time treatment.
dosing: The usual dose is 10 mg per kilogram (mg/kg) of your body weight, given as a single IV infusion over 60 minutes. Your doctor or healthcare provider will calculate the exact dose based on your weight. You only receive this medicine ONCE — there is no repeat dosing schedule.
missed_dose: Because bezlotoxumab is given as a single one-time dose by a healthcare provider, a missed dose works differently than with daily medicines. If you miss or need to reschedule your infusion appointment, call your doctor's office or infusion center as soon as possible to reschedule. Try not to delay too long, as this medicine works best when given during your antibiotic treatment for C. diff.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. It is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. The medicine is kept refrigerated at 2°C to 8°C (36°F to 46°F) until it is ready to be used. It should not be frozen or shaken.
what_to_avoid: There are no specific foods, drinks, or activities you must avoid because of this medicine. However, to help your recovery from C. diff: wash your hands frequently and thoroughly with soap and water (not just hand sanitizer) to prevent spreading the infection; avoid unnecessary use of antibiotics in the future, as they can raise your risk of C. diff coming back; stay well hydrated, especially if you still have diarrhea. Talk to your doctor before starting any new medicines or supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you experience any of the following after receiving this medicine: trouble breathing or shortness of breath; chest pain or tightness; fast or irregular heartbeat; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; dizziness or feeling faint; nausea or vomiting during or after the infusion; skin rash, hives, or itching. Also call your doctor if your C. diff symptoms (such as watery diarrhea, stomach pain, or fever) do not improve or get worse after completing your antibiotic treatment.
when_it_works: Bezlotoxumab starts working right away in your body after the infusion, but you may not notice immediate changes in how you feel. Its main job is to prevent C. diff from coming back after your antibiotic treatment is finished. Most people see the benefit over the weeks following their treatment — studies showed it significantly reduced the chance of C. diff returning within 12 weeks compared to people who did not receive it. Continue taking your antibiotic for C. diff exactly as prescribed — bezlotoxumab does NOT replace antibiotics.
special_populations: Elderly patients (65 years and older): This medicine can be used in older adults, but older patients and those with weakened immune systems are more likely to get C. diff again, which is exactly why this medicine may be especially helpful for them. Heart failure patients: If you have congestive heart failure (CHF), tell your doctor before receiving this medicine. Studies showed a higher rate of death in CHF patients who received bezlotoxumab, particularly those with severe heart failure. Your doctor will carefully weigh the benefits and risks for you. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: It is not known if this medicine harms an unborn baby or passes into breast milk. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding so you can make the best decision together. Kidney or liver problems: Dose adjustments are generally not needed, but always tell your doctor about all your health conditions.
